newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seen stepping up sugar imports.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seen stepping up sugar imports.

text.p: Pakistan, already planning to import 500,000 tonnes of sugar in the fiscal year to next June, may have to buy even more to satisfy strong demand, dealers said on Monday.
Food and Agriculture Minister Nawab Yousaf Talpur said last week that Pakistan was considering buying another 200,000 tonnes of refined sugar for delivery in September and October.
This would be in addition to about 300,000 tonnes already shipped or ordered for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), he said.
The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan has arranged to import 175,000 tonnes and private dealers have bought 125,000 tonnes to make up for a crop shortfall of about 300,000 tonnes.
"Pakistan is likely to continue sugar imports this year to meet its growing needs," said one dealer, who asked not to be named. He said an extra 300,000 tonnes might be needed.
Dealers cite sugar smuggling as another pressure on supplies. Some 200,000 tonnes of sugar were smuggled from Pakistan to nearby Iran and Afghanistan in 1995/96, dealers say.

Domestic sugar production sank to 2.47 million tonnes in 1995/96 from three million in 1994/95 and an official of the Islamabad-based Pakistan Sugar Mills Association (PSMA) said weather conditions meant no big increase was likely this year.
"I see no dramatic change in sugar production in 1996/97 as weather conditions are not favourable to the sugarcane crop," said the official, who asked not to be named.
Rain, floods and cloudy weather could slow the normal growth of sugarcane in Punjab and Sindh provinces, he said. Some officials, however, said the rain could make the cane juicier.
Crop forecasts conflict, even though the start of the sugarcane crushing season is only about a month away.
Former PSMA chairman Altaf Saleem said he expected output to rise to 2.7 million tonnes, roughly matching consumption, from 2.47 million in 1995/96, when consumption reached 2.65 million.

Some mill owners said domestic production could fall this year because of lower recovery from sugarcane. The recovery rate fell to 9.19 percent in 1995/96, when farmers sold unripe cane to mills early in the season, from 9.65 percent in 1994/95,
"I see lower production of sugar in 1996/97," Haji Hasham Haji Ahmed, owner of a sugar mill in Sindh, told Reuters.

Sugar importer Mohammad Siddiq of Aminsons in Lahore said it was too early to be sure, but argued that output could rise as farmers were growing more cane to cash in on higher prices. Sugar sells for 20 rupees per kg, up from 13 rupees a year ago.
Dealers have bought 2.182 million tonnes, or more than 88 percent, of the sugar produced in 1995/96, leaving stocks of only 287,000 at sugar mills as of August 15, PSMA figures show.
